k-1.x_notes: Has the same six problems as Y, and all of them check out: P1 mixes tileable shapes with odd-area and even-area-but-unbalanced ones (the 8-triangle trapezoid has 5 up and 3 down); in P2 the fewest greens are 2, 3, 4; P3 shapes have 2 and 3 tilings; in P4 the fewest blocks are 3, 3, 4; the P5 game answers are 1st, 2nd, 1st, 1st, 2nd; P6 has 6 tilings. Strengths: the 'Use only the small blocks' rule matters because 2x/3x blocks are in the room. P3 separates the two shapes with a rule and says which to do first. Bold '1st/2nd' is easier for kindergartners to read. P6 gives 8 full-size copies, so children can leave each tiling in blocks and compare them physically to spot duplicates. Weaknesses: P6 spills onto a 7th page headed 'More copies for Problem 6' and needs many blue blocks at once. P3 offers 3 copies for a shape with only 2 tilings, which can mislead.
k-1.y_notes: Same problems with the same correct mathematics, and P1-P5 are essentially identical to X. Weaknesses: there is no rule against upscale blocks. P3 puts 7 copies of two different shapes on one page without separating them. P5's 'first/second' is harder for K readers. P6 gives one full-size board plus eight half-inch drawing copies, and drawing rhombi on half-inch triangles is fiddly and abstract for kindergartners, though it does leave a record and needs fewer blocks.
k-1.reason: The packets are nearly identical. X's small-blocks rule, clearer P3 layout and full-size copies for the P6 tiling hunt keep the K-1 work more concrete and easier to run.

grades-2-3.x_notes: The mathematics is the same as Y's and correct. P1/P2 boards cover odd area, colour imbalance and the hourglass, which is balanced overall but has two unbalanced halves joined only at a point. Triangles of side 2-5 need 2-5 greens. Chevrons never beat blues. P6 can be solved (two size-3 triangles bridged by a down-triangle plus one up gives 13 up and 7 down). In P7, any one-up/one-down removal from the side-2 hexagon is tileable (checked). Strengths: every page opens with a numbered problem. P4 puts the size-5 triangle together with the 10/100 generalization and the proof on one page, with good writing space. P7 asks only why the failing placements can never work, which grade 2-3 children can explain. Includes the small-blocks rule.
grades-2-3.y_notes: Same problems and correct mathematics. Weaknesses: the P3 size-5 triangle sits on a page with no text or problem label, a continuation children may not connect to P3. P4 (10 and 100) gets only three lines and asks for no explanation, sharing a page with P5. P7's 'explain why your rule is right' also implicitly asks why every one-up/one-down placement works, which is beyond this band. No small-blocks rule.
grades-2-3.reason: The content is identical. X's page structure is cleaner (no unlabeled continuation page, the generalization and proof together) and its P7 explanation request is better pitched for this age.

grades-4-5.x_notes: Same arc as Y: P1 (6 tilings, ribbons give C(4,2)), flips, the A-F flip distances, 4-flip cycle with no odd cycles, ribbons, parity and lower-bound proof, 20 tilings of the side-2 hexagon, and 20 for P8. Strengths: P4 fixes the start at covering A, which is pictured, and gives a recording strip of small hexagons plus lines. Each problem has its own page with ample space. P7 allows 'draw or list', which invites listing ribbon pairs. Includes the small-blocks rule. Weaknesses: P2 has no diagrams, just a large blank area, so children must invent how to organize the coverings (an open method, but harder to start). 'Flip' is only named in P3. The P5 ribbon definition 'from flat edge to flat edge' is terse and leans on the picture.
grades-4-5.y_notes: Same problems and correct mathematics. Strengths: names the flip in P2 and has children build the flip graph on 8 small boards, the representation the kernel highlights. The P5 ribbon procedure is spelled out more clearly. Weaknesses: P2 has children redraw all six P1 coverings and dictates the method. P4 has only two lines and no recording boards for the 4-flip cycle, and is crammed onto one page with P5, which leaves less room for writing ribbons. No small-blocks rule.
grades-4-5.reason: Y's flip-graph prompt and clearer ribbon definition are real pluses. X's dedicated workspace for the flip cycle and roomier, open-method pages serve the 40 minutes slightly better.

overall.reason: The two packets share nearly every problem and diagram, and the mathematics in both is correct and well sequenced, so either would work. X wins narrowly on practical details: the small-blocks rule (upscale blocks will be on the table), full-size copies for the K-1 tiling hunt, one problem per page with adequate workspace, and no unlabeled continuation pages. Y's best feature is the explicit flip-graph task for grades 4-5.
